transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-11-04
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Michael Chen (Redwood AE), Rina Patel (Redwood SE), Aisha Rahman (CTO - Veloria), Tom Bradley (Platform Eng), Keiko Sato (ML Eng)
Shared: Veloria prod ingest diagram (link: https://redwood.ai/shared/veloria-ingest), Redwood quickstart deck (link: https://redwood.ai/deck/veloria-poc)

Summary:
Quick alignment on integration approach for Veloria's embeddings + retrieval pipeline. Primary questions: which deployment mode (Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private) fits their compliance and latency constraints; support for LangChain/LlamaIndex adapters; best patterns for gateway/proxy and per-route quotas; observability hooks and token-level cost reporting.

Topics covered:
- SDK usage and adapter support (LangChain, LlamaIndex)
- Gateway/proxy architecture and best practices for caching + batching
- Rate limits, per-route quotas, and burst handling
- Observability hooks: traces, token-level breakdowns, eval hooks
- Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs (latency, cost, data residency)
- Next steps for pilot and benchmarks

Transcript body:
[00:00:05] Michael Chen: Hey everybody, thanks for joining. Quick roll call, hi I'm Michael from Redwood, AE, and Rina will walk through the technical pieces.
[00:00:12] Aisha Rahman: Aisha here, CTO at Veloria. Tom and Keiko on the call as well. Thanks.
[00:00:20] Tom Bradley: Yep, Tom.
[00:00:23] Keiko Sato: Keiko.
[00:00:28] Michael Chen: Great — the agenda is pretty simple: figure out how your embedding pipeline will talk to Redwood, which SDKs/adapters you'll use, and what constraints you have around SLOs and security. Rina, you wanna kick off?
[00:00:38] Rina Patel: Sure. Quick overview: Redwood provides a hosted API with per-token pricing, Dedicated reserved capacity for predictable throughput, and Private (VPC / on-prem) for strict data residency. For integrations we have native SDKs in Python/Node, first-class LangChain and LlamaIndex adapters, and guidance on running a local gateway or using Redwood's gateway proxy pattern.
[00:01:02] Keiko Sato: When you say "first-class" adapters, does that mean we can drop them into our current LangChain pipeline without forking? We use a mix of LangChain + a light custom wrapper.
[00:01:14] Rina Patel: Right — the adapter is a thin shim that implements the same call signatures LangChain expects. There are two paths: 1) use Redwood SDK directly in your code, or 2) use the LangChain/LlamaIndex adapter which maps the chain calls to Redwood endpoints, including streaming and function-calling. Small caveat: a few community LangChain components assume OpenAI-specific response shapes — we have compatibility layers that translate those.
[00:01:44] Aisha Rahman: Compatibility layer — can you surface that so our engineers can review?
[00:01:48] Michael Chen: Yep, we can share the adapter snippet. Rina will add a short demo.
[00:01:53] Rina Patel: I'll add it to the shared folder and demo in the follow-up.

[00:02:12] Tom Bradley: Our main concerns — we run a high-throughput ingestion for clinical notes. Embedding throughput peaks around 1.2M tokens/day and bursts are common first thing in the morning. Latency target for retrieval queries is ~120ms P95. How do you recommend we route between Hosted and Dedicated?
[00:02:36] Rina Patel: If bursts are frequent and predictable, Dedicated is a better fit — reserved GPU pools give more consistent P95. Hosted is fine for lower, spiky traffic but you will see more variance. Also, caching and prefix/KV cache can help reduce the load for repeated contexts. We can show a cost model calculating when Dedicated breaks even.
[00:02:58] Keiko Sato: For retrieval queries — do you recommend local embeddings store or remote? We currently keep vectors in-house and call our embedder and then store vectors in the vector DB. The encode step is where we're evaluating Redwood.
[00:03:14] Rina Patel: Most customers keep vectors local and call Redwood for embeddings only. That keeps control of vectors and search latency under your DB. We also support generating embeddings via batch endpoints to amortize startup overhead. For low-latency retrieval, you can precompute embeddings and only call for freshness windows.

[00:03:42] Aisha Rahman: Security/regulatory: we need SOC2, SSO (SAML), KMS integration for key management, and audit logs. Also potential on-prem for a subset of workloads. How do those map to Hosted vs Private?
[00:03:58] Michael Chen: Hosted supports SOC2, SAML SSO via SSO integrations and we provide audit logs and a compliance pack. For customer-managed keys and full on-prem we recommend Private — VPC control plane and optional on-prem package. Dedicated can also be VPC-enabled for enterprise. We'll share the compliance matrix.
[00:04:20] Tom Bradley: Good. Also, our network team enforces an egress proxy — we'd want to run a small gateway in our VPC that routes to Redwood to minimize open egress. Is that pattern supported?
[00:04:31] Rina Patel: Absolutely — the gateway/proxy pattern is common. Two flavors: a) lightweight reverse-proxy that forwards requests with token-based auth, or b) a colocated gateway that does batching, local cache and enforces per-route quotas. We have a sample gateway repo that implements backpressure and batch aggregation.
[00:04:53] Keiko Sato: Backpressure is critical. We've seen request storms saturate the embedder and kill downstream DB writes. How does Redwood handle throttling and per-route quotas?
[00:05:04] Rina Patel: Redwood supports per-API-key and per-route quotas. We also expose rate-limit headers and webhook alerts for quota exhaustion. If you run a local gateway, you can enforce stricter per-service quotas and implement token-buckets at the edge. For Dedicated customers we also provide a burst buffer config that allows short bursts beyond committed capacity with transparent billing.

[00:05:36] [00:05:36] Aisha Rahman: You mentioned KV cache earlier — can you explain? We assume you meant KV cache for autoregressive models, how does that help embeddings?
[00:05:45] Rina Patel: Sorry, mixed contexts — KV cache is for generative models to reuse key/value attention states. For embeddings the analogue is prefix caching — if the same document text is requested repeatedly we can serve from cache or use fingerprinting to dedupe requests before hitting the model. For Veloria's embed pipeline, deduping at the gateway and batch embedding will be most effective.

[00:06:16] Tom Bradley: About telemetry — we need trace ids to correlate a token cost to our request and be able to attribute cost per customer tenant. What observability hooks do you provide?
[00:06:25] Rina Patel: We have request-level metadata in our console and an API that returns token breakdowns per request (input tokens, output tokens, compute type). We also emit trace ids and allow customers to pass a correlation_id header. For Dedicated/Private we can push logs to your logging sink or provide integrations with Datadog/New Relic.
[00:06:47] Keiko Sato: Do you provide streaming token-level breakdowns in real-time or only post-hoc?
[00:06:53] Rina Patel: Streaming includes chunked outputs; token-level cost metrics are currently post-hoc via the usage API but we can stream partial usage events for certain customers as part of an enterprise observability add-on.

[00:07:20] Michael Chen: Quick interjection — pricing: we'll send a modeled sheet. It will show hosted per-token rates and Dedicated committed capacity examples. The break-even calculation will include your token distribution and burst profile.

[00:07:32] [00:07:32] Aisha Rahman: For the LangChain integration: our pipeline uses LlamaIndex on top of LangChain in some locations — any special considerations?
[00:07:40] Rina Patel: LlamaIndex tends to manage document stores and chunking. Our LlamaIndex connector supports the indexing and retrieval steps and maps the embedding calls. The common hiccup is text normalization and chunk boundaries; we recommend keeping a consistent tokenizer and version across your embedding generation and retrieval. We'll supply best-practice notes.

[00:08:08] Tom Bradley: On the gateway, would it be possible to do local batching to push to Redwood batch endpoint, and then return results asynchronously? We're comfortable with async writes for embeddings.
[00:08:20] Rina Patel: Yes — the batch endpoints are designed for exactly that. You can POST a batch of texts, get an async job id, and then poll or receive a webhook when embeddings are ready. That reduces per-request overhead and helps throughput.

[00:08:44] Keiko Sato: Any SDK quirks — we use Python 3.11 and Node 20 in parts — will we run into compatibility issues?
[00:08:52] Rina Patel: SDKs support Python 3.8+ and Node 14+. We test against current LTS; Python 3.11 is fine. There are a couple of optional dependencies for streaming players; we'll point those out. Also if you use native C lib tokenizers, ensure compatible versions when you pre-tokenize.

[00:09:12] [00:09:12] Aisha Rahman: Regarding SSO and RBAC — can we map roles to route-level quotas? Eg. internal service accounts get higher per-minute throughput than third-party connectors.
[00:09:23] Michael Chen: Yes — RBAC ties into API keys and roles in the console. You can attach quota policies to roles and API keys, and for Dedicated/Private we can integrate with your SAML provider for entitlement sync. We'll include an example policy in the follow-up.

[00:09:48] Tom Bradley: How are model rollouts handled? We sometimes want to A/B models for quality vs cost. Is that supported in the routing layer?
[00:09:58] Rina Patel: Yes — rollouts are a feature in Redwood Console: canary deploys, A/B splits, automatic fallback to cheaper variants, and per-route model pinning. For Dedicated customers we also provide traffic shaping at the runtime.

[00:10:26] Keiko Sato: Any limits on embedding dimensionality or model sizes we should know about?
[00:10:32] Rina Patel: We support common embedding dims up to 4096, and for very large dims there may be memory/cost implications. We'll confirm supported models and dims in the adapter doc.

[00:10:48] Michael Chen: Let's pivot to a short demo. Rina, can you show the LangChain adapter code snippet?
[00:10:55] Rina Patel: Yep — sharing screen... (snippets)
[00:11:12] [00:11:12] Rina Patel: Example: from redwood import RedwoodClient; rc = RedwoodClient(api_key=os.getenv('RW_KEY')); rc.embeddings.create(["text1","text2"], model='rw-embed-2') — and for LangChain: from langchain import RedwoodEmbeddings (pseudo) — instantiate RedwoodEmbeddings(api_key=...), pass into LlamaIndex/DocumentIngest. Note: we translate response shapes to match LangChain's expectations.

[00:11:46] Keiko Sato: That looks straightforward. Do you do automatic retries on 5xx or do we need to implement?
[00:11:51] Rina Patel: SDKs have configurable retry policies with exponential backoff and idempotency keys for safe retries. For batch endpoints we recommend idempotency tokens.

[00:12:10] Tom Bradley: We're interested in trying a small POC: 100k tokens/day steady, peak 400k, embed batch job nightly, and retrieval latency target 120ms P95. Would Redwood do a trial of Dedicated vs Hosted comparison?
[00:12:28] Michael Chen: Yes — we typically do a pilot where we run benchmark jobs against Hosted and a Dedicated trial instance. We'll set up a test harness and measure P95 and cost-per-embedding. Rina will own the technical runbook.

[00:12:46] Aisha Rahman: What is the timeline to stand up a Dedicated trial? 
[00:12:51] Rina Patel: For Dedicated trial we can provision a small pool in 7–10 business days once contract paperwork is done and network peering set. Hosted tests can start in a day. Private on-prem takes longer — usually a multicloud/ops project.

[00:13:09] [00:13:09] Keiko Sato: A few gotchas from our side: we use a custom request-id header and need the service to echo it back so we can trace through our system; also we want to instrument token-cost per tenant.
[00:13:20] Rina Patel: You can pass X-Correlation-ID and we will echo it. For tenant-level cost attribution, include tenant_id in metadata and we'll surface cost by tenant via the usage API. We'll note that in the runbook.

[00:13:44] Tom Bradley: Does Redwood expose model-level latency histograms we can pull into our Grafana?
[00:13:50] Rina Patel: We can export metrics to your metrics backend (Prometheus pushgateway or Datadog) for Dedicated/Private. For Hosted customers we expose dashboards and a metrics export API as part of observability add-on.

[00:14:12] Michael Chen: Let's capture a few constraints so the follow-up is prescriptive: (1) P95 retrieval <= 120ms; (2) Peak embed throughput 400k tokens/day spikes; (3) Need SAML + KMS + audit logs; (4) Gateway/proxy in our VPC with local batching; (5) Tenant-level cost attribution. Anything missing?
[00:14:34] Aisha Rahman: That's the main list. Also add a pilot success criteria — eg. match retrieval latency and show cost within X% of model.

[00:14:43] Keiko Sato: Also want a runbook for failure modes — if Dedicated pool saturates what's the fallback?
[00:14:50] Rina Patel: Fallback policies: automatic fallback to a lower-cost model or to Hosted cross-region pool depending on policy. We can set hard circuit breakers at the gateway.

[00:15:06] [00:15:06] Michael Chen: Great. Quick question from our side — do you have any internal constraints for data residency (i.e., PII handling) that would push you to Private?
[00:15:16] Aisha Rahman: We handle PHI; some data must remain on-prem or in a dedicated VPC. For initial pilot we can use pseudonymized data but full production will likely require VPC or Private.

[00:15:30] Rina Patel: Understood. We have Private deployments and Dedicated with VPC options for that. We'll include the compliance pack and also an NDA addendum if you need it.

[00:15:46] Tom Bradley: One last thing — billing integration: we use internal chargeback and want to be able to pull per-tenant usage via an API. Is that available?
[00:15:56] Rina Patel: Usage API returns per-request metadata; you can aggregate by tenant_id. For enterprise customers we also provide a billing export CSV that can be ingested into chargeback systems.

[00:16:12] [00:16:12] Aisha Rahman: Okay let's talk schedule: we'll get you the embedding sample and the gateway config by Friday. Can you get pricing and an adapter demo by next Monday?
[00:16:21] Michael Chen: Yes, we'll send pricing by 2025-11-10 and Rina will record a short demo for Keiko.

[00:16:30] Keiko Sato: Cool. A few minutes of open Q&A — how do you handle model updates that change embedding semantics? We need to detect regressions.
[00:16:40] Rina Patel: We have Evaluate and Optimize. You can upload labeled pairs and run regression tests; we also support continuous quality monitoring tied to prompt sets and embedding drift detection. If a model update causes regression we can pin older model versions and notify you.

[00:17:02] Tom Bradley: Would you run periodic re-embedding jobs if model changes?
[00:17:07] Rina Patel: We don't automatically re-embed for you, but we provide the tooling to run mass re-embeds via batch jobs and incremental re-embedding pipelines. We can help size the job during the pilot.

[00:17:22] [00:17:22] Michael Chen: Switching to a slightly more tactical point — your gateway-proxy sample: do you support auth via mTLS or only token auth?
[00:17:30] Rina Patel: We support both depending on deployment. Hosted typically uses token-based auth; Dedicated/Private can support mTLS and mutual peering. We'll include the sample config for mTLS.

[00:17:46] Aisha Rahman: Great. Anything else from the team?
[00:17:50] Tom Bradley: No, that's it.
[00:17:53] Keiko Sato: Nothing else.

[00:18:00] Michael Chen: Okay, we'll wrap. I'll recap in slack and email.

[00:18:05] [00:18:05] Closing remarks and recaps (timestamps jump for brevity)
[00:30:00] Michael Chen: Recap: we'll share pricing + compliance pack; Rina will add LangChain/LlamaIndex adapter snippets and a recorded demo; Tom will share gateway config and token distribution sample; Keiko will run an initial adapter test.
[00:40:00] Rina Patel: Action items assigned in the notes, we will prepare a Dedicated trial runbook and benchmark harness.
[00:52:00] Aisha Rahman: Next meeting tentatively week of 2025-11-17 for adapter deep dive.
[00:57:14] Michael Chen: Thanks everyone — we will follow up with the artifacts and schedule.

Notes on transcription quality: some speaker labels were auto-assigned; a few technical terms may be slightly garbled (eg 'KV cash' vs KV cache) — refer to notes above.
